name: raiseChild.py - Automated Child→Parent Escalation
description: Automates the entire child-to-parent domain escalation chain: DCSync child KRBTGT → enumerate SIDs → forge ExtraSids golden ticket → execute on parent DC. One command replaces the manual lookupsid + ticketer + psexec chain. Use when you have child domain admin and want fastest path to parent domain compromise.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHAT RAISECHILD.PY DOES AUTOMATICALLY ===
raiseChild.py automates the full ExtraSids escalation chain:
  1. DCSync the child DC to get the child KRBTGT hash
  2. Enumerate child domain SID
  3. Enumerate parent domain SID (for Enterprise Admins = RID 519)
  4. Forge a golden ticket with ExtraSids (parent EA SID in ticket)
  5. Use that ticket to psexec the parent DC → get SYSTEM shell
  6. DCSync the parent domain (dump all hashes)

The manual equivalent uses: secretsdump → lookupsid → ticketer → psexec
raiseChild.py replaces all of that with one command.

=== REQUIREMENTS ===
  - Child domain admin or DA credentials
  - Connectivity to both child DC (for initial DCSync) and parent DC (for final exec)
  - -target-exec <parent_dc_ip> specifies where to execute on the parent side

=== OUTPUT ===
  [*] Raising child domain LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
  [*] Performing DCSync ...
  [*] Got KRBTGT hash: <hash>
  [*] Enumerating SIDs...
  [*] Forging golden ticket with extra SID: S-1-5-21-...-519
  [*] Executing on 172.16.5.5 ...
  [!] Launching semi-interactive shell - Ctrl+C to abort
  Microsoft Windows...
  C:\Windows\system32> whoami
  nt authority\system

=== WHEN TO USE MANUAL vs RAISECHILD ===
  raiseChild.py: fastest, one command, exam time savings
  Manual chain: when you need to inspect each step, save the ticket separately,
                or when raiseChild fails (connectivity issues, DNS problems)

=== AFTER GETTING PARENT DC SYSTEM ===
secretsdump.py -just-dc -outputfile parent_hashes INLANEFREIGHT/Administrator@172.16.5.5 -hashes :<nt_hash>

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

recommended.note: Leverage trust data for cross-domain forging.

defense.why_it_works: raiseChild.py chains the full ExtraSids escalation automatically: (1) DCSync the child DC to extract KRBTGT hash, (2) enumerate child and parent domain SIDs via LSARPC, (3) forge a golden ticket with the parent's Enterprise Admins SID (RID 519) in the ExtraSids field of the PAC, (4) use that ticket to authenticate to the parent DC via psexec — the parent KDC trusts the ticket because its inter-realm trust key validates the referral, and the ExtraSids field grants EA privileges.
defense.prerequisites: Child domain admin credentials (or DA). Network connectivity to both child DC (for DCSync) and parent DC (for final execution). DNS resolution or -target-exec IP for the parent DC. Impacket installed.
defense.impact: Fully automated child→parent forest escalation resulting in SYSTEM on the parent DC. From there: secretsdump of the entire parent domain, golden ticket for the parent, complete forest compromise. One command collapses what is normally a multi-step manual chain.
defense.detection: Generates all the same indicators as the manual chain simultaneously: Event 4662 (DCSync) on child DC, LSARPC SID enumeration traffic, cross-domain Kerberos referral with ExtraSids in PAC, Event 7045 (service install) on parent DC, Event 4624 type 3 on parent DC. MDI alerts on both DCSync and the cross-realm golden ticket. The multi-event burst from a single source IP in rapid succession is itself a strong SIEM indicator.
defense.prevention: Enable SID Filtering on the parent-child trust — this is the most direct mitigation (blocks ExtraSids from being honored). Note: disabling SID filtering on parent-child trusts breaks some legitimate cross-domain functionality; evaluate carefully. Reset KRBTGT passwords in all child domains to prevent DCSync data being used. Deploy MDI across all domains in the forest. Child domain compromise should trigger forest-wide incident response.
defense.evasion: The manual step-by-step approach (secretsdump → lookupsid → ticketer → psexec) is more controllable and allows pausing between steps, but generates the same fundamental indicators. raiseChild.py is an automated tool — less evasion-tunable than the manual chain. Use the manual chain when stealth matters; raiseChild.py when speed is priority.
defense.misconfiguration: Domain trusts (especially bidirectional and forest trusts) extend authentication boundaries. SID filtering is often disabled on forest trusts to support legacy applications — but this allows an attacker with Domain Admin in a child domain to forge a golden ticket with ExtraSids claiming Domain Admin SID in the parent/trusted forest. Without SID filtering (SIDHistory filtering), domain boundaries offer no security isolation.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Bidirectional forest trust without SID filtering:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, SIDFilteringQuarantined
# SIDFilteringQuarantined: False  <-- SID filtering DISABLED
# Direction: BiDirectional        <-- both domains trust each other

# Child domain to parent: SID filtering is always disabled by default
# Enterprise Admin SID (S-1-5-21-<root>-519) can be added to ExtraSids
# Golden ticket with ExtraSids = cross-domain privilege escalation
defense.secure_config:
# Enable SID filtering on external/forest trusts:
netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes
# 'Quarantine' = SID filtering enabled — ExtraSids from other domain are stripped

# For child-to-parent trusts (SID filtering can't be enabled without breaking functionality):
# Use Selective Authentication instead of full trust
# Only accounts explicitly granted 'Allowed to Authenticate' can use the trust
netdom trust <ParentDomain> /domain:<ChildDomain> /SelectiveAuth:yes

# Restrict SIDHistory (prevents ExtraSids abuse):
# Audit accounts with SIDHistory:
Get-ADUser -Filter {SIDHistory -like '*'} -Properties SIDHistory

# Monitor cross-forest authentication:
# Event 4769 on parent DC with ticket from child domain user
